name: Don't Go Brocking My Heart Burger - (with broccoli and artichoke hearts)

recipe.history:
Broccoli (Brassica oleracea var. italica) is a proud product of the Italian peninsula, cultivated by the ancient Romans and refined through centuries of agricultural tradition in Calabria and Campania. The word itself derives from the Italian broccolo, meaning "the flowering crest of a cabbage," and the vegetable was prized by Roman emperors who reportedly ate it boiled and seasoned with cumin and coriander. The globe artichoke (Cynara scolymus), meanwhile, traces its roots to the Mediterranean basin — likely originating in North Africa or Sicily — and was enthusiastically adopted by Arab cultivators who brought it to Spain and southern Italy during the medieval period. By the Renaissance, Catherine de' Medici is said to have carried her beloved artichokes from Florence to France, cementing the vegetable's aristocratic culinary status across Europe. Both plants share a lineage steeped in the cuisines of sun-drenched coasts, olive oil, and the kind of unhurried, ingredient-forward cooking that treats vegetables not as a side thought but as the very soul of a dish.

Broccoli made its way to American shores primarily through Italian immigrant communities in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, though it remained largely unknown to the broader American public until the D'Arrigo Brothers Company of California began commercial cultivation and aggressive marketing in the 1920s. It took decades more — and the quiet endorsement of home cooks across the country — for broccoli to become a staple of the American table. Artichoke hearts followed a similar arc: cultivated commercially in Castroville, California (which still calls itself the "Artichoke Capital of the World"), they became accessible to everyday cooks in jarred and canned form by mid-century, finding their way into dips, pasta dishes, and eventually the adventurous world of burger toppings. The American burger, always a democratic and improvisational canvas, welcomed these Mediterranean transplants naturally. Creative cooks discovered that the slight bitterness of broccoli florets, crisped in a hot pan, and the briny, tender richness of marinated artichoke hearts offered a complexity that cut through the fatty depth of a beef patty in exactly the right way.

I remember the first time I truly understood what a burger could be — it was a Tuesday, which matters because Tuesdays have a specific kind of hunger to them, neither the relief of the weekend nor the momentum of Monday. I was standing in a small kitchen with avocado-green appliances that belonged to another era entirely, and someone had roasted a whole head of broccoli in a cast-iron skillet until the edges went almost black and nutty. There were artichoke hearts in a jar on the counter, the good kind packed in olive oil, and a burger patty resting on a wooden cutting board, its interior still blushing pink at exactly 132°F. The combination felt accidental, improvised, a little reckless — and that is what made it sing. That burger tasted like the confidence to throw together what you have, like the particular pleasure of a meal that nobody planned but everyone remembers. Every time I make this burger, I am back in that kitchen, and it is still Tuesday, and everything is just about to come together.

To cook a burger to anything above medium rare is to misunderstand what a burger is. The science is plain: the Maillard reaction does its best and most complex work on the exterior crust in the first two minutes of high-heat contact, developing hundreds of flavor compounds that give a properly seared patty its deep, almost caramelized character. But interior temperature is where the fat does its work. At 130–135°F (54–57°C), intramuscular fat melts into the surrounding meat fibers, carrying fat-soluble flavor compounds through every bite and producing that unmistakable, juicy texture that makes a burger worth eating. Push the patty to medium (145°F) and that fat begins to render out entirely, dripping away into the pan, leaving behind a drier, less expressive piece of meat. Well done is simply a different food — technically beef, spiritually something else. Medium rare is not a preference; it is the state in which a quality beef patty is most fully itself. It respects the animal, the grind, the seasoning, and the cook's effort. Serve your burgers medium rare. There is no other way.
ingredients: 300g (2 1/2 cups) bread flour, plus extra for dusting
1 tbsp sesame seeds (optional, for topping buns)
680g (1.5 lbs) freshly ground beef — 80/20 chuck blend (or 60% chuck / 40% brisket ground together)
1 tbsp neutral oil (such as canola or grapeseed) for searing
1 large head of broccoli, cut into small florets (about 3 cups)
1 can (14 oz / 400g) artichoke hearts in water, drained, or 1 jar marinated artichoke hearts in olive oil
240ml (1 cup) neutral oil (canola or light olive oil)
Salt and white pepper to taste
1 cup baby arugula or fresh spinach
1 large ripe tomato, sliced into 4 rounds
instructions: 1. MAKE THE BUNS — In a large bowl, whisk together the bread flour, yeast, sugar, and salt. In a separate bowl, whisk together the warm milk and egg. Pour the wet ingredients into the dry ingredients and stir until a shaggy dough forms.

2. Turn the dough onto a lightly floured surface. Knead for 2 minutes, then incorporate the softened butter a little at a time, kneading until fully absorbed after each addition. Continue kneading for 8–10 minutes total, until the dough is smooth, elastic, and slightly tacky but not sticky.
3. Place the dough in a lightly oiled bowl, cover with plastic wrap or a damp towel, and let rise at room temperature until doubled in size, about 1 to 1.5 hours.

4. Punch down the dough and divide it into 4 equal portions (roughly 130g each). Shape each portion into a tight, smooth ball by tucking the edges underneath and rolling against the work surface with a cupped hand. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, spacing them 3 inches apart. Cover and let rise again for 45 minutes, until noticeably puffed.

5. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Brush each bun gently with egg wash (1 egg yolk beaten with 1 tbsp water). Sprinkle with sesame seeds if using. Bake for 16–18 minutes, until deep golden brown. Transfer to a wire rack and cool completely before slicing.

6. MAKE THE GARLIC AIOLI — Using the side of a chef's knife, crush 3 garlic cloves with 1/4 tsp kosher salt and work them into a smooth paste by smearing repeatedly with the flat of the blade. In a medium bowl, whisk together the garlic paste, egg yolks, Dijon mustard, lemon juice, and white wine vinegar.

7. While whisking constantly, add the neutral oil in an extremely thin, steady stream — drop by drop at first — until the mixture begins to emulsify and thicken. Once a stable emulsion forms (after incorporating about 1/4 of the oil), you can add the remaining oil in a slow, steady drizzle, whisking continuously. Season with salt and white pepper. Refrigerate until needed.

8. PREPARE THE ARTICHOKE HEARTS — Quarter the drained artichoke hearts. Heat 2 tbsp olive oil in a skillet over medium heat. Add the minced garlic and cook 30 seconds until fragrant. Add the artichoke hearts, dried thyme, salt, and pepper. Cook, stirring occasionally, for 5–7 minutes until the artichokes are lightly golden at the edges. Remove from heat, finish with lemon juice, and set aside.

9. PREPARE THE BROCCOLI — Heat a large cast-iron or heavy skillet over high heat until very hot, about 2 minutes. Add 3 tbsp olive oil and immediately add the broccoli florets in a single layer. Do not stir for 2 minutes — allow them to char and blister on one side. Toss and cook another 2–3 minutes. Reduce heat to medium, add sliced garlic and red pepper flakes, toss to combine, and cook 1 more minute. Season with salt, pepper, and lemon juice. Remove from pan and set aside.

10. FORM THE PATTIES — Remove the ground beef from the refrigerator 20 minutes before cooking. Do not overwork the meat. Gently divide it into 4 equal portions (about 170g each). Loosely form each into a ball, then press into a patty approximately 3/4 inch thick and slightly wider than your buns (they will shrink slightly). Use your thumb to press a shallow dimple into the center of each patty. Season both sides generously with kosher salt, black pepper, and garlic powder immediately before cooking.

11. COOK THE PATTIES TO MEDIUM RARE — Heat a cast-iron skillet or heavy griddle over high heat until it just begins to smoke. Add 1 tbsp neutral oil and swirl to coat. Place patties in the pan — do not press them down. Sear for exactly 2.5–3 minutes on the first side without moving, until a deep brown crust forms. Flip once. Cook for another 2–2.5 minutes on the second side.

12. In the final 60 seconds of cooking, lay one slice of provolone or fontina cheese over each patty. Cover the pan with a lid or foil to melt the cheese. Use an instant-read thermometer to verify the internal temperature reads 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. Remove patties from heat and let rest on a wire rack for 3 minutes — carry-over cooking will bring them to a perfect 133–135°F.

13. TOAST THE BUNS — While the patties rest, slice each bun in half. Place cut-side down in the same skillet (wiped clean) over medium heat with a small amount of butter. Toast for 60–90 seconds until golden and lightly crisp.

14. ASSEMBLE THE BURGERS — Spread a generous tablespoon of garlic aioli on both the top and bottom bun cut surfaces. On the bottom bun, layer in this order: a small handful of baby arugula or spinach, one slice of ripe tomato, a few rings of thinly sliced red onion, the cheese-topped patty, a generous spoonful of sautéed artichoke hearts, and a heap of charred broccoli florets.

15. Finish with a pinch of flaky sea salt over the broccoli and artichoke hearts. Set the top bun in place, press gently, and serve immediately. The burger is at its best in the first 4 minutes — do not wait.
